ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In the diagram to the right a $2 \times 2 \times 2$ cube is made up of four transparent $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cubes and four non-transparent black $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cubes. They are placed in a way so that the entire big cube is nontransparent; i.e. looking at it from the front to the back, the right to the left, the top to the bottom, at no point you can look through the cube. What is the minimum number of black $1 \times 1 \times 1$ cubes needed to make a $3 \times 3 \times 3$ cube non-transparent in the same way?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure is a 2×2×2 large cube composed of small cubes; some small cubes are shown as opaque with gray/black shading, and the white frame-line parts indicate transparency. The illustration explains: as long as a certain line of sight that passes straight through from one face to the opposite face encounters an opaque small cube, this line of sight is blocked; transparent small cubes do not block the line of sight. Then reason: Model the 3×3×3 large cube as coordinates (x,y,z), where x,y,z∈{1,2,3}, and regard the coordinates modulo 3 as residues 1,2,0. In order that it cannot be seen through from front to back, for each fixed (x,y), a line of sight along the z direction must have at least one black small cube. There are 3×3=9 such front-back direction lines of sight. One black small cube can only be located on and block one of these front-back direction lines of sight, so at least 9 black small cubes are needed. Next show that 9 are sufficient. Place black small cubes at positions satisfying z≡x+y (mod 3), where residue 0 corresponds to coordinate 3. Thus for each fixed (x,y), there is a unique z, so each front-back direction line of sight is blocked; for each fixed (x,z), the equation gives a unique y, so each left-right direction line of sight is blocked; for each fixed (y,z), the equation gives a unique x, so each up-down direction line of sight is also blocked. Therefore 9 black small cubes can make the 3×3×3 large cube opaque in all three directions. Combining with the lower bound, the minimum number is 9.

method.method_draft: Model the 3 x 3 x 3 cube as coordinates (x,y,z) with x,y,z in {1,2,3}. From the image, note that a black unit cube blocks a straight line of sight through the big cube, while transparent cubes do not. From the text, the cube must be blocked in all front-back, left-right, and top-bottom directions. There are 9 front-back sight lines, one for each fixed pair (x,y). A single black cube can block only one such front-back line, so at least 9 black cubes are necessary. To show 9 suffice, place black cubes at coordinates satisfying z ≡ x + y mod 3, using residues {0,1,2}. This gives exactly one black cube in every fixed (x,y), every fixed (x,z), and every fixed (y,z) line, so all three viewing directions are blocked. Therefore the minimum is 9.

For a 3 x 3 x 3 cube, looking from the top requires the black cubes to project onto all 9 cells of the top face, so at least 9 black cubes are needed. If exactly 9 are used, then there must be exactly one black cube in each vertical column. Record, for each top-face cell (row, column), the depth at which its black cube is placed. To also block the front-back view, each row must contain the three depths 1, 2, 3. To block the left-right view, each column must contain the three depths 1, 2, 3. Choose a 3 x 3 Latin square of depths, for example rows 1,2,3 / 2,3,1 / 3,1,2. This places 9 black cubes and blocks all required projections, so the minimum is 9.

推理：Interpret the condition by projections. For a 3×3×3 cube to be non-transparent from top to bottom, every one of the 9 top-face positions must have at least one black cube somewhere in its vertical column. Since a single black 1×1×1 cube can occupy only one such vertical column, at least 9 black cubes are necessary.

Now show that 9 are sufficient. If we use exactly 9 cubes, put exactly one black cube in each vertical column. This can be done with a 3×3 Latin square of levels, for example:
1 2 3
2 3 1
3 1 2
Thus there is one black cube in every top-bottom column, and every front-back and left-right line also contains a black cube. Therefore 9 black cubes work, and the lower bound proves it is minimal.
